description: Five CS students from Palestine Polytechnic University (PPU), Hebron, competing at the Nablus event. Challenge: Abandoned but not Forgotten. We're building Robot Stories, an English/Arabic website where NASA's robots on the Moon, Mars and deep space tell kids their own stories, with quizzes and badges. Skills: web dev, .NET, Python, AI and UI/UX. We have a working prototype and a friendly team. Looking for: an illustrator/animator or a storyteller for kids.
summary:
We developed Abandoned but not Forgotten, an interactive, bilingual (English and Arabic) storytelling website for children aged 9–15. It tells the stories of NASA equipment left on the Moon and Mars, and of probes in deep space. Visitors choose a destination, pick one of 21 missions, and follow it chapter by chapter, from launch and landing to its discoveries, how its mission ended, and where it is today.

Each chapter combines a short animated scene, real NASA photos, "Did you know?" facts, a quick quiz and a dated timeline. Every fact links to the NASA page it came from. When NASA sources disagree, the site says so instead of hiding it.

This answers the challenge by turning silent hardware into stories that explain what each machine is, why it was sent and what it found. It matters because these explorers are part of our scientific heritage, yet their stories usually end when the mission does. Our project helps young people, including Arabic speakers, connect with real space science.
details:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive storytelling website for children aged 9–15 about NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars, and spacecraft that travelled into deep space. Visitors start in a living star field and choose a destination: the Moon, Mars, or Deep Space & Beyond. They then pick one of 21 missions, such as the Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle, the Spirit and Opportunity rovers, Viking 1 and 2, InSight, Ingenuity or Pioneer 10. Each mission is told as a journey of short chapters: what the machine is, why it was built, launch, landing, discoveries, how the mission ended, and where it is now. Every chapter combines a short animated scene, real NASA photos with credits, "Did you know?" facts, an "Explore more" section and a quick quiz question, plus a dated timeline for each mission.

Benefits and intended impact

Most people hear about launches and landings, but the stories of these machines usually stop when their missions end. Our site turns them into stories children can follow, showing how real science works step by step. The site is fully bilingual in English and Arabic, with a complete right-to-left layout, so Arabic-speaking children get the same experience. It works on phones and computers, needs no account, and collects no personal data.

Scientific accuracy

Every fact is linked to the NASA or NSSDCA page it comes from (61 sources). Each fact carries an evidence label. When NASA pages give different values, the site says so instead of picking one, and if something is only claimed on the challenge page, we label it that way. The team is running a human fact-check mission by mission: Moon corrections are done and locked, Mars is reviewed, and Deep Space is next.

Tools and technologies

React 18, TypeScript, Vite 5, Tailwind CSS 3 and React Router 6.

Animations built with CSS keyframes.

Mission content stored as structured JSON in two languages, checked by a custom data validator and 27 automated tests (Vitest).

Browser testing with Playwright.

Hosted free on GitHub Pages.

NASA Image and Video Library, NASA Science and NSSDCA as data sources.

An AI coding assistant (Claude Code by Anthropic) for development, research support and quality checks. All facts are traced back to NASA sources and reviewed by the team.

No hardware was used.

What makes it creative

Each spacecraft is treated as the main character of its own story, with a beginning, a journey and an ending, rather than as a list of facts. The site follows a journey structure, with chapter progress bars, cinematic scenes and a "What happened next?" ending, and it is honest about uncertainty.

Factors we considered

Age-appropriate language and short chapters.

Accessibility: alt text on every image, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support.

Equal quality in Arabic and English.

Labelling animations as illustrations rather than real footage.

Correct image credits.

Never inventing facts, and keeping decorative objects separate from real missions.
